title_en: Walt Disney Company v. Beijing Publishing House et al. — copyright infringement dispute
keywords_en: Civil; copyright infringement dispute; first instance; intermediate people's court; Beijing; legal person; foreign-invested enterprise; Copyright Law; validity of copyright licensing contract; publisher's duty of care; distributor's infringement liability; partially upheld; copyright of cartoon characters; book publishing and distribution; copyright assignment contract; copyright; guarantee; copyright infringement dispute involving Beijing Publishing House et al.
full_text_en:
The Walt Disney Company (USA) v. Beijing Publishing House et al. — Copyright Infringement Dispute

Plaintiff: The Walt Disney Company (USA), domiciled at 500 South Buena Vista Street, Burbank, California, USA.

Authorized Representatives: Li Jingbing, Yu Xiaofeng, lawyers from Beijing Beidou Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Publishing House, domiciled at No. 6, Beisanhuan Middle Road, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Zhu Shuxin, Director.

Authorized Representatives: Wang Yadong, lawyer from Beijing Junhe Law Firm; Ren Liying, lawyer from Beijing No.5 Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Children's Publishing House, domiciled at No. 6, Beisanhuan Middle Road, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Zhu Shuxin, Director.

Authorized Representatives: Wang Yadong, lawyer from Beijing Junhe Law Firm; Ren Liying, lawyer from Beijing No.5 Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Distribution Agency of the General Store of Xinhua Bookstore, domiciled at No. 54, Beilishi Road, Xizhimenwai, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Tian Hui, Manager.

Authorized Representatives: Peng Xuefeng, Zang Wei, lawyers from Beijing Dacheng Law Firm.

Third Party: Great World Publishing Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 13, Dongjiaominxiang, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Nie Gongcheng, Chairman.

Authorized Representative: Cai Zhensheng, Editor-in-Chief of Great World Publishing Co., Ltd.

The plaintiff, The Walt Disney Company (USA), filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No.1 Intermediate People's Court against the defendants Beijing Publishing House, Beijing Children's Publishing House, and Beijing Distribution Agency of the General Store of Xinhua Bookstore regarding a copyright infringement dispute.

The plaintiff, The Walt Disney Company (USA) (hereinafter referred to as Disney) alleged that the cartoon character images such as Mickey Mouse, Cinderella, Peter Pan, and Snow White are artistic works created by Disney and have been registered for copyright in the United States. The defendants, Beijing Publishing House, Beijing Children's Publishing House (hereinafter referred to as Children's Publishing House), and Beijing Distribution Agency (hereinafter referred to as Beijing Distribution Agency), without the plaintiff's permission, published, distributed, and sold nine books of the "Disney Moral Story Series" (hereinafter referred to as the "Series"), including "Bambi Makes Friends" and "Peter Pan's Victory," which reproduced Disney's cartoon images, thereby infringing Disney's copyright. The plaintiff requested the court to order the defendants to immediately cease the publication, distribution, and sale of the aforementioned Series, provide a written guarantee not to further infringe the plaintiff's copyright, publish a public apology in newspapers distributed both domestically and internationally in China, and compensate the plaintiff for economic losses of over RMB 1,770,000.

The defendants, Beijing Publishing House and Children's Publishing House, argued that the cartoon images involved in the Series, which they began publishing in August 1991, had obtained the right to use through a "Contract for Transfer of Chinese Simplified Edition Publication Rights for Disney Children's Books" (hereinafter referred to as the "Transfer Contract") signed with Maxwell Communications Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Maxwell). Furthermore, according to their agreement with Great World Publishing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Great World), Great World was responsible for providing proof of copyright confirmation from the foreign party for the Series, and they had no obligation to independently contact the foreign party regarding copyright matters. Since Great World failed to provide the authorization from the foreign party, resulting in the infringement of Disney's copyright, the responsibility rests entirely with Great World, and Great World should be added as a defendant.

The defendant, Beijing Distribution Agency, argued that as a distributor, it had no obligation to review the copyright legality of the books. Current laws and international conventions do not stipulate that distributors should bear liability for infringement. Moreover, there was an agreement with Beijing Publishing House that in the event of an infringement dispute, Beijing Publishing House would be responsible.

The third party, Great World, stated that it merely acted as an intermediary to contact domestic publishers for the transfer of copyright at Maxwell's request and was not a party to the copyright transfer. The contract signed with Beijing Publishing House was limited to the purchase of films and the forwarding of royalty payments. Furthermore, this contract was signed one year before the effective date of the "Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the People's Republic of China and the Government of the United States of America on the Protection of Intellectual Property" (hereinafter referred to as the "Sino-US MOU"). After that date, Beijing Publishing House never requested any proof from Great World, and Great World was completely unaware that Beijing Publishing House continued to publish and distribute the books after the Sino-US MOU took effect. Therefore, Great World should not bear liability for infringement.

The Beijing No.1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts after trial:

(1) Children's Publishing House is a secondary brand of Beijing Publishing House and is essentially an editorial department of Beijing Publishing House responsible for publishing children's books; it is not an independent legal entity. Maxwell was a company registered in Hong Kong and declared bankruptcy in July 1993. Great World was established in February 1990 as a joint venture between Maxwell and the Beijing Xuanwu Consulting Service Department of World Affairs Press. Maxwell's equity has since been transferred to Ning Shi Law Firm (USA).

(2) "A Book About Kindness," "A Book About Helping Others," and "A Book About Courage" were registered for copyright in the United States on November 30, 1987. The image of Mickey Mouse was registered for copyright in the United States on September 2, 1987, with the copyright belonging to Disney. The cartoon images in the nine books of the Series published by Beijing Publishing House in three print runs (August 1991, November 1992, and November 1993)—"The Kind Cinderella," "Snow White's New Home," "Peter Pan's Victory," "Bambi Makes Friends," "Dumbo's Road to Success," "The Adventures of a White Spotted Dog," "Alice in Wonderland," "Faithful Lady," and "The Prince Rescues Sleeping Beauty"—were identical to the original English versions provided by the plaintiff. The cover of each of the nine books in the Series featured the image of Mickey Mouse and bore the title "Disney Moral Story Series," with each book priced at RMB 2.

(3) Disney and Maxwell entered into an agreement on August 19, 1987, which stipulated: "Disney grants Maxwell a non-exclusive right to publish Chinese language publications, limited to the sale of storybooks featuring Disney theme park characters in China. The license granted under this agreement shall not be transferable by any act of the licensee or through legal proceedings. The contract term is from October 1, 1987, to September 30, 1990, with a 180-day sell-off period after the expiration date." Through the introduction of Great World, Maxwell and Children's Publishing House signed the "Transfer Contract" on March 21, 1991, which stated: "Maxwell, authorized by Disney, holds the exclusive publication rights for Disney children's books in Chinese and has the right to handle copyright trade matters for such books. Maxwell transfers Disney's authorization to Children's Publishing House." On the same day, Children's Publishing House and Great World signed an agreement to implement the "Transfer Contract," stipulating that Children's Publishing House commissioned Great World to finalize the text, typeset, and produce printing plates for the Disney children's books; Great World guaranteed to provide qualified color films for the simplified Chinese character version; and Great World was responsible for providing Children's Publishing House with the foreign party's confirmation of the copyright contract for the Disney Series, serving as the legal basis for Children's Publishing House's copyright ownership in China. Subsequently, Great World received RMB 69,750 for the film expenses of the Series, with costs of RMB 59,312.40, resulting in a profit of RMB 10,437.60.

(4) On March 11, 1992, Children's Publishing House submitted the "Transfer Contract" to the Beijing Copyright Bureau for review. As no authorization letter from Disney was provided, the Bureau did not complete the registration procedures. Children's Publishing House subsequently failed to complete the registration procedures.

(5) Additionally, on February 1, 1991, Beijing Publishing House and Beijing Distribution Agency signed a working agreement stipulating that for books sold on an exclusive distribution basis, the notation "Distributed by Xinhua Bookstore" should be marked. The agreement also stipulated: "For the publication of foreign works or books, the publishing house shall sign a publication contract with the copyright owner, submit the contract to the copyright administration authority for review and registration, and obtain a registration number before submitting the book to Beijing Distribution Agency for subscription and publication arrangements. Otherwise, all foreign-related copyright disputes arising from publication, distribution, and sale shall be solely the responsibility of the publishing house." Although the copyright page of the Series stated "Distributed by Beijing Distribution Agency of Xinhua Bookstore," it should have read "Published and Distributed by Beijing Publishing House, Sold by Xinhua Bookstore."

(6) During the trial, the court commissioned Beijing Tianzheng Certified Public Accountants to audit the profitability of Beijing Publishing House and Beijing Distribution Agency regarding the publication and distribution of the Series. The results were as follows:

After the Sino-US MOU took effect on March 17, 1992, Beijing Publishing House published 118,200 copies of the Series. Of these, it distributed 41,779 copies, had 33,341 copies in inventory, and commissioned Beijing Distribution Agency to distribute 43,080 copies. Beijing Publishing House's production costs were RMB 116,353.86, taxes were RMB 6,679.01, and it actually incurred a loss of RMB 40,197.50. Beijing Distribution Agency's total distribution revenue was RMB 62,850.17, distribution purchase cost was RMB 56,112.60, taxes paid were RMB 738.53, and gross profit was RMB 5,999.04.

Beijing Distribution Agency objected to the above audit findings, arguing that distribution expenses should be deducted to determine the distribution gross profit, but the audit did not deduct such expenses.

(7) Disney paid a total of RMB 869,564.80 in legal fees to law firms in Beijing and the United States for this litigation. It also incurred translation fees of RMB 1,280 and transportation fees of RMB 1,216.60.

The above facts are confirmed by documentary evidence including the publishing house registration certificate, an explanatory note from Children's Publishing House, a letter from the Enterprise Registration Division of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, copyright registration forms, original books, the Series, the agreement between Disney and Maxwell, the Transfer Contract, the agreement between Great World and Children's Publishing House, Great World's invoices, a certification from the Beijing Copyright Bureau, a certification from the National Copyright Administration, the publication and distribution working agreement, a certification from Beijing Publishing House, the audit report, fee receipts, as well as the statements of the parties involved.

The Beijing No.1 Intermediate People's Court held that:

(1) Pursuant to the provisions of the Sino-US MOU, works of U.S. nationals are protected under Chinese law from March 17, 1992. Disney holds copyright in the artistic works involved in this case, including the cartoon images of Mickey Mouse, Cinderella, Snow White, Peter Pan, Bambi, Dumbo, the White Spotted Dog, Alice, and Lady. Any commercial use of these cartoon images without Disney's authorization constitutes infringement.

(2) Although Disney once authorized Maxwell to publish and distribute picture books containing Disney's cartoon images in China, it did not authorize Maxwell to transfer the publication and distribution rights of these works to others. Therefore, Maxwell's transfer of the publication and distribution rights of Disney's works to Children's Publishing House when its final sell-off period was about to expire, on one hand, infringed Disney's rights and interests, and on the other hand, constituted a fraud against Children's Publishing House. This contract is legally invalid.

(3) Legally, Maxwell's fraudulent act of signing the "Transfer Contract" with Children's Publishing House was the primary cause of this infringement incident, making Maxwell the main responsible party. Given that Disney has not filed suit against Maxwell and that Maxwell declared bankruptcy in July 1993, Maxwell's liability in this case is not pursued. However, considering that the infringement liability in this case arises from multiple causes resulting in a single consequence, the amount of compensation to be paid by each defendant should be correspondingly reduced.

(4) Children's Publishing House was overly hasty in entering into the publication contract with Maxwell without examining whether Maxwell had the right to transfer the publication rights of Disney's works. According to the provisions of Document No. (90) Quan Zi 3 of the National Copyright Administration, "Regulations for the Strict Implementation of Relevant Rules on Copyright Trade with Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macao": "After March 1, 1988, any copyright trade contract with Taiwan, Hong Kong, or Macao entered into by any unit or individual, whether for transferring copyright or authorizing use, or for receiving such transfers or authorizations, must be submitted to the copyright administration authority for review and registration. If not reviewed and registered, the required procedures shall be completed before March 1, 1990. Contracts that have not been reviewed and registered are null and void." Children's Publishing House, without a legal copyright certification and after the national copyright authority refused to register the contract, still failed to conduct a review and did not complete the registration procedures in accordance with relevant national regulations before publishing and distributing picture books containing Disney's cartoon images. Its subjective fault is evident. Since Children's Publishing House is not an independent legal entity, its liability shall be borne by Beijing Publishing House.

(5) Article 3, Item 7 of the Sino-US MOU stipulates: "... (1) Liability shall not be imposed for commercial-scale use of original U.S. works or copies thereof occurring before the establishment of bilateral copyright relations between China and the United States. (2) For such use occurring after the establishment of bilateral copyright relations, the provisions of laws and regulations shall fully apply. ..."

Beijing Publishing House's three print runs of the Series for profit constitute "commercial-scale use" of U.S. works. Since the first print run occurred before the effective date of the Sino-US MOU, it is not pursued. The second and third print runs occurred after the effective date of the Sino-US MOU and constitute acts of infringement as defined in Article 46, Item (2) of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China: "reproducing and distributing a work for profit without the permission of the copyright owner" and Item (3): "publishing a book in which another person has exclusive publication rights." These acts constitute infringement and Beijing Publishing House shall bear infringement liability.

(6) Beijing Distribution Agency participated in the sale of the Series from Beijing Publishing House's second and third print runs. According to Article 5, Item (5) of the Implementing Regulations of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, sale is a form of distribution. Whether the sales method is "exclusive distribution" or "general distribution" is a matter of business model and does not affect whether the act legally constitutes infringement. As a distributor, it has a duty of care regarding legal defects in the subject matter it distributes. The working agreement between Beijing Distribution Agency and Beijing Publishing House stipulated that for the publication of foreign works or books, the publishing house must sign a publication contract with the copyright owner, submit the contract to the copyright administration authority for review and registration, and obtain a registration number before submitting it to Beijing Distribution Agency for subscription and publication arrangements; otherwise, all foreign-related copyright disputes arising from publication, distribution, and sale would be solely the responsibility of the publishing house. In practice, however, Beijing Distribution Agency did not verify whether Beijing Publishing House had obtained the registration number from the copyright administration authority. This indicates that although Beijing Distribution Agency noted the relevant national regulations when signing the agreement, it failed to actually implement them. Therefore, Beijing Distribution Agency is deemed to have subjective fault. Pursuant to Article 106, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, it shall bear infringement liability for its acts of distributing infringing books. Beijing Publishing House shall bear joint and several liability for Beijing Distribution Agency's illegal sales. Given that the working agreement stipulated that all foreign-related copyright disputes would be solely the responsibility of the publishing house, and since Beijing Publishing House is already a defendant in this case, the compensation liability for infringement of Beijing Distribution Agency shall be borne by Beijing Publishing House. However, this does not relieve Beijing Distribution Agency of its obligation to cease infringement, and the illegal profits obtained from the infringement should also be confiscated. Beijing Distribution Agency's objection that distribution expenses should be deducted from the gross profit is unfounded, as distribution expenses were incurred in the course of the infringement.

(7) The agreement between Great World and Children's Publishing House stipulated that Great World was responsible for providing Beijing Publishing House with the foreign party's confirmation of the copyright contract for the Disney Series, serving as the legal basis for Children's Publishing House's copyright ownership in China. Regarding the term "foreign party's confirmation" here, this court accepts Great World's interpretation that it refers to confirmation by Maxwell. Since the agreement stipulated Great World's guarantee obligation, Great World should have carefully examined whether the "confirmation by the foreign party, i.e., Maxwell" was legal and effective. Moreover, Great World acted as an intermediary in the signing of the contract between Children's Publishing House and Maxwell, which played a significant role in enabling Maxwell's fraud to succeed. Great World's defense that it was merely an introducer and did not bear guarantee liability is not accepted. Although there is no evidence to prove malicious collusion between Great World and Maxwell, the fact remains that Great World failed to fulfill its duty of care as a guarantor, constituting subjective fault. Pursuant to Article 106, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law, Great World shall bear partial liability for the economic losses incurred by Beijing Publishing House due to its liability for compensation in this infringement incident, and its illegal profits shall also be confiscated.

(8) Disney's claims of infringement against the above defendants are established and are supported. However, the amount of damages claimed and the reasons provided contain certain unreasonable elements. The minimum guaranteed royalty of USD 100,000 is based on agreements entered into with parties in Hong Kong and Taiwan, but the economic conditions in Mainland China differ significantly from those regions. Moreover, the minimum guaranteed royalty is a matter agreed upon by the parties and can only be referenced by the court, not used as a basis for judgment. Therefore, this court does not adopt it. As for the claimed amount of legal fees, some portion does not pertain to this litigation and is not considered. For the legal fees used for this litigation, the court can only order the defendants to bear them by reference to relevant regulations. Given that Disney's request for "an order that the defendants provide a written guarantee not to further infringe the plaintiff's copyright" is not a legally prescribed form of civil liability, it is not supported.

Accordingly, on May 18, 1995, the Beijing No.1 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment:

1. Beijing Publishing House and Beijing Distribution Agency of the General Store of Xinhua Bookstore shall immediately cease the publication and distribution of the "Disney Moral Story Series" from the date this judgment takes effect.

2. Beijing Publishing House shall, within 60 days from the date this judgment takes effect, publish a public apology to the plaintiff, The Walt Disney Company (USA), in a newspaper published domestically and distributed nationwide in China.

3. Beijing Publishing House shall, within 15 days from the date this judgment takes effect, pay a lump-sum compensation of RMB 227,094.14 to the plaintiff, The Walt Disney Company (USA).

4. Great World Publishing Co., Ltd. shall, within 15 days from the date this judgment takes effect, pay compensation of RMB 90,837.66 to Beijing Publishing House.

5. All other claims of the plaintiff, The Walt Disney Company (USA), are dismissed.

Big World Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment of the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. The grounds for its appeal were: (1) The agreement signed between Big World Company and Children's Publishing House, and the contract signed between Maxwell Company and Children's Publishing House, were both acts that occurred before the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum. The court of first instance erred in investigating Big World Company's conduct before the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum. (2) Big World Company provided the film to Children's Publishing House before August 1, 1991, and no person or unit raised any objection within two years after that act occurred. Children's Publishing House requested that Big World Company be added as a defendant in this case in July 1994, by which time the statute of limitations had already expired. The court of first instance, disregarding this fact, added Big World Company as a third party in this case and ordered Big World Company to pay compensation to Beijing Publishing House, which lacked legal basis. (3) The infringing acts in this case were the second and third publications of the "Series" by Beijing Publishing House after the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum. From the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum, ongoing commercial-scale uses of American works should automatically terminate, and prior contracts should cease to be performed. Children's Publishing House had submitted the "Simplified Chinese Copyright Transfer Contract" signed with Maxwell Company to the Beijing Copyright Bureau for review, but registration was refused, which indicated that the contract was invalid and should not be performed. However, Children's Publishing House, knowing that performing the contract would necessarily constitute infringement of Disney Company's works and would be subject to legal sanctions, especially after the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum, disregarded the legal consequences and published the "Series" twice more. This was an independent intentional infringement by Children's Publishing House itself, and the tort liability should be borne by it alone. The first-instance court's decision that Big World Company should bear part of the compensation liability for Children's Publishing House's infringement was unjust. Therefore, Big World Company requested the Beijing High People's Court to set aside item (4) of the first-instance judgment, and the litigation costs were to be borne by Beijing Publishing House. Disney Company, Beijing Publishing House, and the Beijing Distribution Office of Xinhua Bookstore General Store accepted the first-instance judgment.

After trial, the Beijing High People's Court held that, since the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum, works of American citizens are protected by Chinese law. Any commercial use of the artistic works involved in this case, for which Disney Company holds the copyright, without authorization from Disney Company, constitutes infringement. Children's Publishing House, by entering into a contract with Maxwell Company without verifying whether Maxwell Company had the right to transfer the publication rights of Disney Company's works, should bear certain responsibility for that invalid contract. After the Beijing Copyright Bureau refused to register the contract due to the lack of copyright certification, Children's Publishing House knew that the contract should not be performed, but it neither conducted a review nor supplemented the relevant registration procedures, and it unauthorizedly published and distributed the "Series" containing Disney cartoon characters. Especially after the effective date of the Sino-US Memorandum, Children's Publishing House, disregarding the legal consequences of infringing Disney Company's copyright, published the "Series" twice for profit, demonstrating clear subjective fault. The economic losses suffered by Disney Company due to the above infringement shall be compensated by Children's Publishing House. Since Children's Publishing House is a non-independent legal entity and lacks the capacity of a civil subject, its tort liability shall be borne by its superior authority, Beijing Publishing House.

Beijing Distribution Office, by distributing the "Series" for Beijing Publishing House without verifying whether the "Series" published by Beijing Publishing House was lawful, constituted an infringement of Disney Company's copyright. In view of the work agreement signed between Beijing Publishing House and Beijing Distribution Office, which stipulated that all foreign-related copyright disputes shall be handled by the publishing house, the tort compensation liability of Beijing Distribution Office shall be borne by Beijing Publishing House. The illegal gains obtained by Beijing Distribution Office from distributing the "Series" shall be confiscated.

The contract concluded between Big World Company and Children's Publishing House on March 21, 1991, for the purpose of implementing the "Simplified Chinese Copyright Transfer Contract" signed between Children's Publishing House and Maxwell Company, had a performance period of three years. During the performance of this contract, Big World Company did not, in accordance with the contract, provide Children's Publishing House with the copyright contract for the Disney series confirmed by the foreign party, as the legal basis for Children's Publishing House to enjoy the copyright within China. On March 17, 1992, the Sino-US Memorandum came into effect, and works of American nationals have been protected by Chinese law since March 17, 1992. Under these circumstances, Big World Company should have taken the initiative to negotiate with Children's Publishing House regarding its inability to perform its obligation under the contract to provide the Disney copyright contract confirmed by Maxwell Company, and should have taken necessary remedial measures or terminated the contract between them to avoid continued performance leading to infringement of Disney Company's rights. However, Big World Company's omission acquiesced in the occurrence of the infringing result, and it shall bear partial financial responsibility for the consequences of Beijing Publishing House's infringement. The contract signed between Big World Company and Children's Publishing House on March 21, 1991, had a performance period of three years. The court of first instance added Big World Company as a third party in this case based on that contract, and this did not exceed the statute of limitations. Therefore, the grounds of appeal raised by Big World Company cannot be fully sustained. In summary, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Beijing Publishing House and Beijing Distribution Office committed infringement, and correctly ordered the confiscation of the illegal gains of Beijing Distribution Office and Big World Company, and these aspects shall be affirmed. However, the finding that Big World Company should bear a guarantee liability for Children's Publishing House was erroneous, and the compensation liability imposed on Big World Company in favor of Beijing Publishing House based on this erroneous finding was obviously excessive and shall be corrected. Accordingly, pursuant to the provisions of Article 153, paragraph 1, subparagraph (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court rendered the following judgment on December 19, 1995:

(1) Affirm items (1), (2), (3), and (5) of Civil Judgment (1994) Zhong Jing Zhi Chu Zi No. 141 of the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court.

(2) Set aside item (4) of Civil Judgment (1994) Zhong Jing Zhi Chu Zi No. 141 of the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court.

(3) Big World Publishing Co., Ltd. shall pay compensation of RMB 45,418.83 to Beijing Publishing House within 15 days from the effective date of this judgment.
